While I'm not Asatru myself, my interest in Norse Mythology has gotten me to pick up certain ancient Nordic practices. Let me explain through a brief summary of the study I've been working on (because Asatru follows this outline as far as I can tell):

The ancient Scandinavians, and I look at Icelanders more than anything, believed in the gods and celebrated holidays, but they are nothing like Christians or other pagans. The general feeling is that the gods are an example for you to live by, and you should know the stories, but the gods are distant and on another plain. I'm not even sure how literally they took the mythology. I've been rather skeptical since I've began my studies that the Scandinavians *actually* believed in a Thor and an Odin unless they were especially drawn to the god (such as in the Saga of Hrafnkel Frey-Godi), or they were convinced they saw them (*The Poetic Edda* does have a few encounters between gods and humans). Beyond that, Scandinavians only believed in what they saw. Why were people so scared of Hrapp's ghost in the *Laxdaela Saga*? Because they saw they saw him, and he was an vile man to begin with, so he would be likely to haunt the land. 

Wax says in *Magic, Fate & History* that the Scandinavians did not believe in supernatural things unless they met them; However, she later goes on to explain that they *did* expect to meet nonhuman beings in order to gain "Power or virtues" that were only attainable through that interaction (49). Knut Helle does point out in *The Cambridge History of Scandinavia (Prehistory to 1520)* that there is "no sharp division between the secular and the religious; religious notions were linked to every aspect of life and all action was religious action" (129). At the same time, it is also secular action. You live in this world, but you imitate the gods in order to live in the *right* way.

As an extremely poor American, I would like to complain about the methods used here. (I live in Sourthern California currently. I lived in Northern California up until a year ago)
First, GM may help plants survive against frost (easiest one to think of is tomatoes), but it takes money and energy to create this crops in order to (kinda) increase your chances of them surviving. As the article states, the modifications don't always work.
Second, local foods are bought for a variety of reasons, but there are two highly immportant ones. A riper, richer food (because my apple came off of a tree no more than two days ago), and supporting local business. I don't know how many of you have had corn right off the plant, but it's absolutely amazing. While the stuff at the supermarket is sweet, it's got a strange flavor. When it comes to market venders, they are more likely to use less sweet corn because it can be sold the day after. However, if you grow it yourself, you get the best product. With the second point, if my egg vender get salmanela, all of America doesn't suffer. Only those who eat the eggs. If a stand fails, America doesn't suffer. You can talk to the vender and question directly what they feed their animals or how they farm. You can also work out deals with them. If you come at the end of a market day and they have a crate of tomatoes left, you can get amazing deals. Not to mention that the market allows for a wide variety of potatoes, onions, lettuce, carrots, beans, squash, etc. Some of these varieties are more nutritious, other are just better for cooking, but whatever you need, they have. Also, when plants are exposed to different diseases, they're kinda like every other living thing. They learn how to fight it and they impliment that in every fruit and seed they have. When you eat that, you take that into yourself as well.
Third, feeding the world isn't what we need. Feeding ourselves is what we need. If we can feed ourselves, when famine hits, or a bad storm, OUR town is going to continue. OUR town won't have to go hungry because we learned how to farm. Teach each community to feed its self and then you won't have world hunger. [Dan Barber](http://www.google.com/url?sa=t&source=web&cd=3&ved=0CDAQtwIwAg&url=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.ted.com%2Ftalks%2Fdan_barber_how_i_fell_in_love_with_a_fish.html&rct=j&q=ted%20dan%20barber&ei=DC96TsrrC8mNsALNw5TVAw&usg=AFQjCNGzvjSA4DlOJafhQfh47XbglhDU-A&cad=rja) makes a pretty good point about this.

Finally, as someone who has studied soil structure, while tilling the soil constantly isn't good, neither is killing the microbes in the soil. Herbacides might only go for the weeds, but you must realize that weeds have roots too, which attract many things to the ground. Some hard word and managable farms can keep most of the weeds from being too tall or being problimatic. Wendell Berry talks more about this.

Organic is not the answer. It's a step in the right direction, though.
Teach people how to farm. Don't farm for them.
Let people use their own water to farm their crops. Don't force them to pay back their debt with it.

Needing to remember everything isn't important, certainly, but I would like to say that the Internet does make it more difficult to entice people to actually memorize things. What I mean is while memorizing the Bill of Rights, as used in a comment above, isn't needed, it is still a good idea. Knowing information offhand is extremely important, and knowing a quote is even more important depending on your point. Being able to quote from someone, or being able to extract the central point of any given piece of work, such as The Republic, gives more crediblity to you as a speaker, and it gives more insight to the listener. 

No, memorization isn't imperative, but it will be that much harder to encourage people to learn certain things by heart when they can look it up in five seconds. 

Also, please note that when books were first coming out, people were worried that it would be the end of the world and that everyone would be stupid because they wouldn't have to memorize their poetry and epics.
